orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling her story to Lockwood. It is the same summer of 1797, the night of Joseph's visit and the early morning after, and Edgar must decide what to do about his nephew.

notes.n: In this chapter 'Mr. Linton', 'Mr. Edgar', 'my master' and 'uncle' all mean Edgar. Plain 'Linton' means the boy.

notes.g: Spend time with him from now on.

notes.t: remain in ignorance of his proximity
notes.g: Not know how close by he is.
Here 'Linton' is the boy, Isabella's son.
notes.n: His father is Heathcliff, so he is going to live with the father he has never met.

notes.m: 'Hearty' meant healthy and vigorous, not cheerful or filling.

notes.t: He had business to keep him in the north
notes.g: A kind white lie by Nelly.
How naughty it was to be unwilling.

notes.n: Heather is the low, purple-flowered shrub that covers the moors.

notes.g: The easy pace of Cathy's pony, Minny.
notes.n: A canter is between a trot and a gallop.

notes.g: From which a light mist rose.

notes.t: on the skirts of the blue
notes.g: At the edge of the sky.

notes.t: a respectable house: the next best in the neighbourhood
notes.g: A decent gentleman's house, second only to the Grange.

notes.t: Hareton Earnshaw—that is, Miss Cathy’s other cousin, and so yours in a manner
notes.g: Hareton is Cathy's cousin through her mother; Linton is her cousin through her father.
notes.n: So Hareton and Linton are not related by blood. That is why Nelly says 'in a manner': in a way.

notes.t: unless a morbid touchiness kindled them
notes.g: Unless an unhealthy, oversensitive irritability lit them up.

notes.t: not a vestige of her sparkling spirit
notes.g: Not a trace of his mother's lively spirit.
'Master' was the polite title for a young boy of good family.

notes.t: three hundred miles is a great distance
notes.g: A long way, several days' journey by coach.
notes.n: Isabella lived in the south, near London.

notes.t: the carved front and low-browed lattices
notes.g: The carved stonework over the door and the low, deep-set windows with small panes.
notes.n: Lockwood described the carvings over the front door in Chapter I.

notes.t: the straggling gooseberry-bushes and crooked firs
notes.g: Untidy fruit bushes and wind-bent fir trees.
notes.n: Lockwood noticed the stunted firs bent by the north wind in Chapter I.

notes.t: his private feelings entirely disapproved of the exterior of his new abode
notes.g: Privately, he didn't like the look of his new home at all.
The inside might make up for it.

notes.t: the family had just finished breakfast
notes.g: Farm households rose very early, especially in summer.
notes.n: It is only half-past six in the morning.
Haymaking means cutting and drying grass in summer to feed the animals through the winter.
Heathcliff calls his son 'property' and 'it'.

notes.tr: Surely he's swapped with you, master, and that's his girl!
notes.n: Probably Joseph's joke that the boy is so girlish that Edgar must have sent his daughter instead.
'Yon' means that one there; 'lass' is a girl.

notes.t: stared his son into an ague of confusion
notes.g: Stared at his son until the boy shook with confusion.
notes.n: An 'ague' is a fever with shivering fits.

notes.t: reared it on snails and sour milk
notes.g: Raised him on feeble, nasty food (a sneer at how weak he looks).

notes.m: 'Sanguine' means optimistic. Nothing to do with blood here.

notes.n: 'Thee' and 'thou' were the familiar forms, used in Yorkshire to children, family and inferiors.

notes.t: Thou art thy mother’s child, entirely

notes.n: To 'pule' is to whine or cry feebly.

notes.g: A child's love and respect for a parent.
A wicked, worthless woman: vicious abuse.
notes.m: Then 'slut' could mean a dirty, slovenly woman as well as an immoral one. Either way it is a harsh insult.

notes.g: At least you can blush, so you're not completely bloodless.
notes.n: Probably a sneer at cowardice: a coward was called 'white-livered'.

notes.m: Here it means 'look after you', though 'do for' could also mean 'ruin'. Heathcliff may enjoy the double meaning.

notes.g: The nobody at the Grange: Edgar.
notes.n: A 'cipher' is a zero.

notes.t: this thing won’t be settled while you linger about it
notes.g: The boy won't settle down while you hang around.

notes.t: he’s all you have akin in the wide world
notes.n: Heathcliff was a foundling with no known family (Chapter IV).

notes.g: Keeping all his love for myself.

notes.n: 'Calf' was slang for a stupid, clumsy lad.

notes.t: my son is prospective owner of your place
notes.g: My son is next in line to own Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: In Chapter XVI Nelly regretted that old Mr. Linton's will passed the estate to his daughter Isabella's line rather than to Edgar's daughter. Edgar has no son, so Isabella's son is the heir.

notes.t: I should not wish him to die till I was certain of being his successor
notes.g: He wants the boy to live until the property is sure to pass to Heathcliff through him.

notes.t: my descendant fairly lord of their estates
notes.g: My child the rightful owner of their lands.

notes.t: my child hiring their children to till their fathers’ lands for wages
notes.g: His son as master, paying their children to farm their own families' land.
notes.n: Heathcliff's revenge turns the class order upside down. 'Till' means to plough and farm.

notes.g: Put up with the pup (the boy).

notes.t: preserve the superior and the gentleman in him, above his associates
notes.g: Keep him a gentleman, ranked above the others in the house.
notes.n: Compare Hareton, who was never taught to read or write (Chapter XVIII).
Whey is the thin, watery, pale liquid left over when milk is curdled to make cheese.

notes.g: A bowl of porridge made with milk.
notes.n: Probably oatmeal porridge, the everyday food of northern farms.

notes.m: 'Homely' meant simple and plain, and a 'mess' was a serving of food, not a muddle.

notes.t: his underlings to hold him in honour
notes.g: His servants to treat the boy with respect.

notes.tr: Can't eat it? But Master Hareton never ate anything else when he was a little one, and what was good enough for him is good enough for you, I should think!

notes.g: A little one; a small child.

notes.t: Is there aught ails th’ victuals?
notes.g: Is there anything wrong with the food?
notes.n: 'Victuals' (said 'vittles') means food.

notes.tr: Well! That fussy lad says he can't eat it. But I suppose that's right! His mother was just the same: we were almost too dirty to sow the grain for making her bread.
notes.n: Joseph sneers that Isabella thought everyone at the Heights too dirty for her.

notes.m: In Britain 'corn' means grain such as wheat or oats, not American maize.

notes.t: acquainting him with the turn Heathcliff’s humour has taken
notes.g: Telling him about Heathcliff's change of mood.
notes.m: 'Humour' here means mood or temper, not comedy.

notes.t: timidly rebuffing the advances of a friendly sheep-dog
notes.g: Nervously pushing away a friendly sheepdog.

notes.t: too much on the alert to be cheated
they did not suffer him to come forth
notes.g: They didn't let him come out.
Got the pony moving at a trot.
My short time looking after him was over.
